summary: A pointer is a variable that holds the memory address of another object. Pointers let C share data without copying it, build linked structures, return multiple results from functions, and reach hardware registers.

sections.heading: What a pointer is
sections.body: Every object lives at an address. The address-of operator `&x` produces it and the dereference operator `*p` reads or writes the object a pointer refers to. The pointer's type tells the compiler how many bytes `*p` touches and how to interpret them.

sections.heading: Declaring and initializing
sections.body: Declare with `type *name;`. The `*` means 'pointer to' in a declaration and 'follow the pointer' in an expression. Initialize at declaration, either to a real address or to NULL.
bullets: Print addresses with `%p` and cast to `void *`; print the pointed-to value with the type's own specifier.

sections.heading: Size of a pointer
sections.body: All data pointers on a given platform have the same size because they only store an address: 4 bytes on 32-bit systems and 8 bytes on 64-bit systems. `sizeof(p)` is the pointer's size; `sizeof(*p)` is the size of the object it points to.
sections.code: printf("%zu %zu %zu\n", sizeof(char *), sizeof(int *), sizeof(double *));  // 8 8 8 on x86-64

sections.heading: Why pointers matter
bullets: Pass-by-reference: a function modifies the caller's variable through its address.
Dynamic memory: `malloc` returns a pointer to heap storage.
Data structures: linked lists, trees, and graphs are nodes joined by pointers.
Efficiency: pass a pointer to a large struct instead of copying it.

sections.heading: Where pointers go wrong
bullets: Dereferencing NULL or a wild pointer is undefined behavior (usually a segmentation fault).
Reading or writing past the end of an array.
Losing the only pointer to heap memory (leak).

subtopics.title: Types of special pointers
subtopics.summary: NULL, void, wild, and dangling pointers.

bullets: NULL pointer: points to nothing; check it before use.
void pointer: generic address holder; cast before dereferencing and no arithmetic.
Wild pointer: declared but never initialized, so it holds garbage.
Dangling pointer: refers to memory that was freed or left scope.

sections.body: A pointer is itself a variable and has an address, so you can point at it. A `**` parameter lets a function change which object the caller's pointer refers to, for example when allocating on the caller's behalf.
sections.code:
void alloc(int **out) { *out = malloc(sizeof **out); }
int *p; alloc(&p);   // p now points to heap memory

sections.body: Read the declaration right to left.
bullets: `const int *p`: the int cannot be modified through p; p can be re-pointed.
`int *const p`: p cannot be re-pointed; the int can be modified.

subtopics.title: Arrays and pointers
subtopics.summary: An array name decays to a pointer to its first element.

sections.body: `a[i]` is defined as `*(a + i)`. In most expressions the array name becomes `&a[0]`, but `sizeof(a)` still gives the whole array's size, which is the main difference from a pointer.

takeaways: A pointer's own size is fixed per platform; the pointee's type sets how memory is read.
Always initialize pointers and check for NULL before dereferencing.
Most C memory bugs are pointer bugs: wild, dangling, out of bounds, or leaked.
